transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, uh, I see Marcus, Sofia, Daniel, and Priya. Great. Well jump into the cost numbers first.
[00:21] Marcus: Yep, thanks Alex. Were mostly here to understand where we land on tokens per dollar and what kinds of latency tradeoffs were gonna accept. Our SLAs are 200 ms p50 and 500 ms p95 ideally.
[00:34] Priya: Cool, Ill start with the numbers we ran last night. Baseline hosted run — mixed prompt set, average seq 256 — gave roughly 1,200 tokens per second per dollar at our default batching (auto-batch size ~16). Thats tokens/sec/$, so to translate to $/1M tokens is in the sheet.
[00:52] Sofia: Sorry could you repeat that number? 1,200 tokens per second per dollar?
[00:57] Priya: Yeah, sorry, 1,200 tokens per second per dollar for the baseline. If we enable more aggressive batching (up to 64), we measured up to ~3,300 tokens/sec/$ but at the cost of median latency shifting from ~120 ms to ~400 ms for tail prompts.
[01:20] Marcus: Right, so batching helps throughput but kills latency - that tradeoff is clear. Our main worry is p95 tail for chat flows.
[01:28] Alex: Exactly, and one lever that helps without increasing cost too much is caching. We ran prefix and KV caching on a subset — top-100 prompts — and saw token usage drop about 28% overall, which translates to similar cost savings.
[01:43] Daniel: Is that from deduping prefixes or from KV reuse?
[01:46] Priya: Mostly KV cache hits; prefix caching handled repeated system messages. So combined its around 25-35% reduction depending on real traffic duplication. For a real production mix with templates and system prompts, expect the higher end.
[02:02] Sofia: How reliable is the KV cache across shards? We have distributed traffic across regions and are worried about cache warming time.
[02:09] Priya: Good question — cache locality matters. In hosted mode we keep caches warm per serving pool; if you route by region we can replicate hot keys or use sticky routing. Cache warm-up cost is small but for cold-starts you can see spikes. Thats where dedicated helps because you can pin a pool to your traffic and get much higher steady-state hit rates.
[02:29] Marcus: Ok, show me the numbers comparing hosted vs dedicated.
[02:31] Priya: Sure — quick summary: hosted baseline tokens/sec/$ ~1,200; dedicated (reserved GPUs, mixed A100-ish profile) measured at ~2,800 tokens/sec/$ at our default quantization (int8). If we push quantization to int4 for non-chat workloads we saw up to ~3,800 tokens/sec/$ but quality risk increases.
[02:50] Alex: Note on dedicated: those numbers assume commit pricing and a steady utilization above ~60%. If utilization drops we need to include reserved cost amortization which can make per-token cost worse.
[03:02] Marcus: Makes sense. Daniel: what about fallbacks — if dedicated is saturated do you spill to hosted and how does that affect cost predictability?
[03:10] Priya: Yes we support smart routing: policy-based spillover to hosted or other variants. That adds complexity to unit economics because you get blended rates; the cost model sheet includes blended scenario examples.
[03:22] Marcus: Can you walk through an example blended scenario?
[03:25] Alex: Yeah, we have a short example in the sheet. If 80% of traffic uses dedicated at 2,800 tokens/sec/$ and 20% spills to hosted at 1,200 tokens/sec/$, the blended becomes about 2,360 tokens/sec/$. You can flip the mix in the spreadsheet.
[03:42] Sofia: Also we need to understand the effect of long-context prompts. Some of our flows hit 4k token context windows intermittently. How does that change numbers?
[03:50] Priya: Long context increases memory working set and reduces batch depth due to memory constraints; tokens/sec/$ tends to drop maybe 20-40% depending on kernel efficiency. We measured a 30% drop at 4k vs 512 tokens on the same hardware.
[04:06] Marcus: Hmm. So for our mixed workload maybe the effective tokens/sec/$ will be lower than the short-context numbers.
[04:11] Alex: Right which is why Marcuss team sharing the request distribution is critical — we can reweight the cost model to your mix.
[04:18] Daniel: Any notes on quantization quality drop? We saw hallucinations increase a bit in int4 for code generation.
[04:24] Priya: Yes, int4 is workload sensitive. For pure NLU/classification it's usually fine; for generative code or long reasoning it can degrade. We recommend a hybrid: int8 for chat/dialogue, int4 for embeddings-only or rerankers. Also Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles per route.
[04:41] Marcus: What about throughput per GPU — tokens/sec absolute numbers?
[04:45] Priya: On an A100-like config we saw roughly 6M tokens/hour at baseline batching; which converts to the tokens/sec/$ numbers with the cost assumptions. The sheet has per-GPU throughput rows.
[04:55] Sofia: Latency targets — can you keep p95 under 500 ms with a mix of caching and batching?
[05:00] Priya: Yes, with aggressive caching you can keep p95 ~250-450 ms while improving tokens/sec/$ by 20-30%. The trick is cache hit rate and avoiding large batch windows on tail requests.
[05:11] Alex: One pragmatic approach we propose: keep a small fast pool for low-latency interactive chat (p95 target), and a larger batch-optimized pool for background or lower-slo requests. Routing by route/endpoint works well.
[05:24] Daniel: Will that complicate our instrumentation and costs?
[05:27] Alex: Somewhat, but Redwood Console gives per-route cost & latency breakdown so you can observe and re-route.
[05:33] Marcus: Any big differences in observability between hosted and dedicated?
[05:36] Priya: Observability is similar; dedicated gives deeper metrics and full control plane logs in your VPC if you choose private. Hosted still provides token-level cost breakdowns and traces.
[05:47] Sofia: We’re also concerned about encryption/KMS for logs and audit. Do you have SOC2+/ISO stuff?
[05:53] Alex: Yes, SOC 2 and ISO are available; we’ll share the security pack. For dedicated/private you can bring your own KMS and we capture audit logs per request. I will include SOC2 evidence in the follow-up.
[06:06] Marcus: Back to cost: what's the sensitivity if cache hit rate is only 10% vs 50%?
[06:12] Priya: If hit rate is 10% you get minimal savings — maybe 3-5% lower cost overall. At 50% hit rate you can see 20-35% lower tokens consumed. The model in the sheet has sliders for hit rate and batching.
[06:25] Daniel: Any real-world numbers from other customers to benchmark?
[06:28] Alex: We’ve seen a range — ecom/retail templates often get 30-40% caching wins; document processing maybe 10-20%. We can anonymize examples.
[06:38] Marcus: Great. For the next run we want two scenarios: 1) Hosted optimized with caching + moderate batching to meet p95 <= 500ms, 2) Dedicated reserved pool with commit pricing and mixed quantization to minimize $/1M tokens. Can you produce both with cost per 1M tokens and tokens/sec/$?
[06:56] Priya: Yep, we’ll produce both. Expect dedicated to show ~2,800 tokens/sec/$ in our baseline numbers and hosted optimized ~1,500-1,800 tokens/sec/$ with caching and careful batching.
[07:11] Sofia: Please make sure the dedicated scenario includes amortized reserved cost assumptions.
[07:15] Alex: Will do. Also, we noticed one anomaly in the last run — a spike in latency due to KV eviction; Priya, can you explain?
[07:23] Priya: Yeah, during that run a memory pressure event caused aggressive eviction and then lots of cold misses. We’ve improved eviction policy since then; also warming routines help. We recommend pre-warm if you know the hot keys.
[07:37] Marcus: Pre-warm adds operational steps — are there automations?
[07:40] Priya: Yes, we can script warmers or pre-fill caches from your recent logs. We'll include a sample script.
[07:47] Daniel: About mixing quantization per route — how granular can that be?
[07:51] Alex: You can route per endpoint and set quantization profiles per model/route. Redwood Optimize can recommend per-route profiles automatically.
[07:58] Marcus: Ok good. Anything else on cost levers?
[08:01] Priya: You can also use response chunking and stopping tokens smarter. For example, if you can early-stop or apply heuristics you reduce tokens consumed. Also caching at tokenizer-level for static prefix tokens helps.
[08:14] Sofia: For the benchmarking, do you need us to run synthetic load or do you want production replay?
[08:19] Priya: Production replay is best for cache hit realism. If you can share anonymized logs or a sampled traffic file that would be ideal. Synthetic helps for load extremes.
[08:28] Marcus: We can provide a sampled bucket of traffic. I’ll coordinate with Sofia.
[08:33] Alex: Great — action items recap coming. Any final Qs?
[08:36] Daniel: One small one — billing granularity, can we get per-route breakdown in billing export?
[08:41] Alex: Yes, per-route cost export is available in CSV; we’ll attach an example.
[08:45] Marcus: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[08:47] Alex: Alright we’ll follow up with the sheet, SOC2 pack, and bench results. Meeting end.
